content: An incomplete miscarriage occurs when not all the products of conception are expelled through the cervix. To remove the retained tissues, medical procedures such as curettage or vacuum aspiration are commonly employed. However, the anaesthetic techniques used to facilitate these procedures have not been systematically evaluated to determine which approach provides the best outcomes for patients. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of various anaesthetic techniques, including general anaesthesia, sedation or analgesia, regional anaesthesia, paracervical block (PCB), or different combinations of these methods, for the surgical evacuation of an incomplete miscarriage. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, and LILACS, up to January 23, 2012. Additionally, reference lists of retrieved studies were reviewed. The inclusion criteria were limited to all published and unpublished randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or cluster-RCTs comparing any anaesthetic technique for this procedure. Quasi-randomised trials and studies available only as abstracts were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion and evaluated the risk of bias. Data extraction was performed independently and cross-checked for accuracy. Seven trials involving a total of 800 women were included in the analysis. The comparisons revealed significant clinical heterogeneity, and due to differences in the randomisation units, the trials were not combined. Instead, individual trial results were reported in detail. Approximately half of the trials were found to have an unclear or high risk of bias in several domains. None of the trials reported data on maternal mortality. Regarding postoperative pain, the use of PCB did not demonstrate improved pain control when compared to sedation/analgesia or to no anaesthesia/no analgesia. However, in one trial comparing PCB with lidocaine versus PCB with saline solution, significant differences were observed in favour of the lidocaine group for reducing moderate or severe postoperative pain (risk ratio [RR] 0.32; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.18 to 0.59). When opioids were used, postoperative nausea and vomiting were more frequently reported in two trials comparing opioids to PCB. Conflicting results were observed in two trials regarding the need for blood transfusion. The authors concluded that the choice of anaesthesia for this procedure should continue to be guided by factors such as availability, effectiveness, safety, side effects, the practitioner's preference, costs, and the woman's preferences. Until more robust evidence becomes available to support the superiority of one technique over another, these considerations should remain central to clinical decision-making.
